right_atrium.name: Right Atrium
right_atrium.description: Upper-right chamber that receives oxygen-poor blood returning from the body and passes it to the right ventricle.
facts: Receives blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus.
Contains the sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart's natural pacemaker.
Empties into the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve.
Has thin muscular walls because it only pumps blood a short distance.

left_atrium.name: Left Atrium
left_atrium.description: Upper-left chamber that receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and passes it to the left ventricle.
facts: Receives blood from the four pulmonary veins.
Empties into the left ventricle through the mitral valve.
Sits at the back of the heart, close to the oesophagus.
Atrial fibrillation often starts near where the pulmonary veins join it.

right_ventricle.name: Right Ventricle
right_ventricle.description: Lower-right chamber that pumps oxygen-poor blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs.
facts: Forms most of the front (anterior) surface of the heart.
Its wall is thinner than the left ventricle's because the lung circulation has lower pressure.
Receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve.
Pumps into the pulmonary circulation.

left_ventricle.name: Left Ventricle
left_ventricle.description: Lower-left chamber and the heart's main pumping chamber; it pushes oxygen-rich blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and the whole body.
facts: Has the thickest muscular wall of the four chambers, often around 1 cm in adults.
Forms the apex (pointed tip) of the heart.
Receives blood from the left atrium through the mitral valve.
The share of blood it ejects per beat is the ejection fraction; about 50-70% is typical in healthy adults.

aorta.name: Aorta
aorta.description: The body's largest artery. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the rest of the body.
facts: Starts at the aortic valve and rises as the ascending aorta.
Curves over as the aortic arch, which gives off branches to the head and arms.
Continues down through the chest and abdomen as the descending aorta.
The coronary arteries branch from its root, just above the aortic valve.
In adults it is roughly 2.5-3 cm wide near the heart.

pulmonary_trunk.name: Pulmonary Trunk
pulmonary_trunk.description: Short, wide artery leaving the right ventricle that splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries, carrying oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
facts: One of the few arteries that carries oxygen-poor blood.
Begins at the pulmonary valve.
Divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries, one for each lung.
Shown in blue here by the common teaching convention for oxygen-poor blood.

superior_vena_cava.name: Superior Vena Cava
superior_vena_cava.description: Large vein that returns oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest to the right atrium.
facts: Formed where the left and right brachiocephalic veins join.
Has no valve where it enters the right atrium.
Drains blood from the upper half of the body.

inferior_vena_cava.name: Inferior Vena Cava
inferior_vena_cava.description: The largest vein in the body; it returns oxygen-poor blood from the legs, abdomen and pelvis to the right atrium.
facts: Runs up the abdomen to the right of the aorta.
Passes through the diaphragm before entering the right atrium.
Drains blood from the lower half of the body.

pulmonary_veins.name: Pulmonary Veins
pulmonary_veins.description: Veins that carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the left atrium.
facts: There are usually four: two from each lung.
They are the only veins in adults that carry oxygen-rich blood.
They have no valves where they enter the left atrium.

tricuspid_valve.name: Tricuspid Valve
tricuspid_valve.description: Valve between the right atrium and right ventricle that stops blood flowing back into the atrium when the ventricle contracts.
facts: Usually has three leaflets (cusps), which gives it its name.
Its leaflets are held by chordae tendineae attached to papillary muscles.
It is an atrioventricular (AV) valve, like the mitral valve.

mitral_valve.name: Mitral Valve
mitral_valve.description: Valve between the left atrium and left ventricle that stops blood flowing back into the atrium when the ventricle contracts.
facts: Has two leaflets, so it is also called the bicuspid valve.
Named after a bishop's mitre because of its shape.
Its closing is part of the first heart sound ('lub').
In mitral valve prolapse the leaflets bulge back into the atrium.

aortic_valve.name: Aortic Valve
aortic_valve.description: Valve between the left ventricle and the aorta that lets blood out to the body and stops it flowing back into the ventricle.
facts: Normally has three semilunar cusps.
About 1-2% of people are born with a bicuspid (two-cusp) aortic valve.
Its closing is part of the second heart sound ('dub').
Narrowing of this valve is called aortic stenosis.

pulmonary_valve.name: Pulmonary Valve
pulmonary_valve.description: Valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk that lets blood out to the lungs and stops it flowing back.
facts: Has three semilunar cusps, like the aortic valve.
Its closing also contributes to the second heart sound.
It works at lower pressure than the aortic valve.

coronary_arteries.name: Coronary Arteries
coronary_arteries.description: Arteries running over the heart's surface that supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen-rich blood.
facts: The left and right coronary arteries branch from the root of the aorta.
The left anterior descending (LAD) artery runs down the front of the heart between the ventricles.
Blockage of a coronary artery can cause a heart attack (myocardial infarction).
They fill mainly while the heart muscle relaxes (diastole).
